description: Lie back, pull your knee up, and read the pinch. Your Hip Rotation Test grades the deepest joint in your body, the one that decides how you squat, sit, and climb. Five mistakes keep hips pinching for years. Here is the quiet-knee line, the ball-and-socket story, and the range work that gives the joint its room back.

scenes.narration: Lie on your back, one leg long, and draw the other knee up toward your chest with both hands, slowly, like you are folding the leg away. Keep going until the movement honestly stops, then read the front of your hip, deep in the crease where leg meets body. Is it quiet? A stretch in the back of the leg? Or a PINCH, a blocked, jammed feeling right in the crease, as if something is being squeezed that should not be? Rate any pinch from zero to ten, note how far the knee travelled before it arrived, then test the other side, because hips are rarely twins. That is your Hip Rotation Test. The hip is the deepest, strongest joint you own, and the one whose complaints people misread longest, blaming backs and groins for what the socket is saying. Remember your pinch number and your tighter side. At the end, I grade them.

scenes.label: A KNEE THAT REACHES QUIETLY
scenes.narration: Here is the line. A knee that travels all the way to your chest with nothing but a pleasant stretch is a hip with room to spare. A pinch arriving only in the last stretch of the movement is the common pattern: a joint that owns most of its range and gets crowded at the very end, usually trainable with the work in this episode. A pinch that arrives EARLY, blocking the knee far from your chest, or a pinch that is sharp rather than jammed, means the joint is crowded or irritated, and forcing depth is exactly the wrong response. One honest qualifier before anyone panics: hip sockets are shaped differently from person to person, genuinely, bone-deep differently, and some hips will never fold like a gymnast's. Your grade is against your other side and your own history. A pinch that is new, growing, or one-sided deserves more respect than a lifelong, symmetrical quirk.
scenes.sub: quiet to chest: full room - late pinch: crowded end - early/sharp: irritated

scenes.narration: The hip is a ball on the end of your thigh bone, turning inside a deep cup in your pelvis, sealed by a ring of cartilage called the LABRUM that keeps the joint smooth, stable, and pressurised. Folding your knee to your chest rolls that ball deep into the cup, and the front of the joint needs clearance for the manoeuvre: bone sliding past bone with the seal gliding between. When the pinch arrives, something in that front corner is being crowded, compressed between the moving parts, and it complains the way anything squeezed complains. This is why hip pain so often feels deep, vague, and impossible to point at with one finger: the structures live centimetres under the surface, behind muscle, in the body's basement. You cannot rub this joint better. You can only change the geometry of how it moves, the strength of the muscles steering the ball, and the positions you ask it to live in. Room is the therapy.

lines: centre the ball as it rolls.
beats.title: THE STEERING CREW

scenes.narration: Here is the hopeful mechanism: the ball does not roll in its socket on rails. It is STEERED, moment by moment, by the deep muscles around the hip, small rotators and stabilisers that keep the ball centred as it turns. When that steering crew is weak or asleep, the ball drifts forward in the socket during deep bends, crowding the front corner sooner, and the pinch arrives early. Train the crew and the same depth arrives with the ball centred and the corner clear, which is why two people with identical bones can have completely different pinches. This reframes the whole condition: an early pinch is often not a damaged joint but an unsteered one. The work that follows from that is unglamorous and effective: rotation practice through comfortable range, deep hip strengthening, and squat patterns adjusted, stance a little wider, toes a little out, to the geometry your socket prefers. Centre it, do not jam it.

beats.text: SIT WITH VARIETY, NOT A THRONE

scenes.narration: Two practical levers decide your hip's daily life. The first is GEOMETRY. Squat depth is not a moral quality; it is a negotiation with your socket's shape. A slightly wider stance, toes turned out a touch, a box that sets your depth where the pinch stays silent: these are not cheats, they are the correct engineering for your particular joint, and strong people have trained entire careers inside their own geometry. The second lever is POSITIONS. The hip spends its day where you park it: one chair, one car seat, one couch corner, always the same folded angle. Joints stiffen into their parking. Vary the positions, sit on the floor sometimes, stand for calls, let the hip visit extension as often as flexion, and the joint keeps the whole map instead of one postcode. Depth is negotiable. Variety is not.

Your advantage is that hip steering is bodyweight work, and your bodyweight is the lightest load in the room. Rotations, controlled leg lowers, squats inside your own geometry: you can practice them daily, in high volume, with the attention this subtle joint demands, while a heavier athlete pays more for every rep and rushes the learning. There is an ego advantage too, and it matters here. The lifter with the most to prove is the one forcing depth his socket hates, chasing a photograph instead of a function. You have nothing to prove to a barbell. You can train the geometry you actually own, get genuinely strong inside it, and let the pinch retire quietly. Hips reward the honest and punish the theatrical. Your build makes honesty cheap.
Now steer it with me. Stance a little wide, toes a little out, squat only as deep as the hip stays quiet, stand tall. Forty seconds on, twenty off, three rounds. Go.

The five mistakes that keep hips pinching for years. One: forcing depth through the pinch, treating a crowded corner like a door to shoulder open, which irritates the seal you are trying to protect. Two: copying someone else's squat, their stance, their depth, their angles, on your differently shaped socket. Three: stretching the pinch harder, jamming the front of the joint in the name of mobility. Four: the parked workday, one folded position for eight hours, then surprise that the joint only knows that position. Five: ignoring a pinch that is new and one-sided, the pattern that deserves actual assessment rather than another mobility video. The thread: this joint heals with room, steering, and variety, and every mistake removes one of the three. And the standing line of this season: hip pain with clicking and catching, pain that wakes you at night, a leg that gives way, or a pinch that keeps growing, see a professional if it persists. Deep joints hide real pathology, and they reward early, proper imaging.

beats.text: QUIET TO CHEST = ROOM TO SPARE

scenes.label: THEN WE FOLD THE LEG AGAIN
scenes.narration: So, your grade. An early or sharp pinch means assess, do not force: train in the quiet range, build the steering crew, and get professional eyes on it if it does not settle. A late pinch, arriving only at the end of the fold, is the crowded end-range grade, the most trainable one here: geometry, steering work, and positional variety usually buy real room within a season. A quiet trip to the chest means room to spare; keep the variety habit and spend your ambition on strength. Whatever your number, you now know the question your hip is asking. Not how deep can you go, but how well is the ball being steered on the way. Put your pinch number in the comments. Just the number. We fold the leg again in thirty days.
scenes.sub: early/sharp: assess - late pinch: steer it - quiet: room to spare

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same floor, same slow fold, and we grade that hip's room again. Subscribe, because next we return to the knee, where the mistakes are different and the tendon keeps a longer memory. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 hip pinch Mistakes That Are Destroying Your hip tissue healing
